articles.title: ‘Embryonic’: lost novel by French film-maker Éric Rohmer is republished
articles.summary: English translation of Élisabeth, the New Wave director’s 1946 book about young lovers in prewar Paris, receives rave reviews as precursor to auteur’s cinematic work. In the dog days of the second world war, 24-year-old Maurice Schérer wrote a tale of young lovers in prewar small-town France.
body: Now – eight decades on from its first publication, 16 years on from its author’s death – Élisabeth belatedly returns from the cold. Republished in an English-language translation by Aaron Kerner, Rohmer’s book has been greeted with glowing reviews, hailed as a lost modernist classic and a crucial origin story for the award-winning director of Claire’s Knee, The Green Ray and My Night at Maud’s. “It would be a rewarding, exciting read even if the identity of its author were unfamiliar,” wrote Richard Brody in the New Yorker. The fact that it’s by Rohmer? That’s the icing on the cake.

“On the one hand, to be honest, the book is a footnote,” says the novelist André Aciman, a longtime Rohmer fan who wrote the foreword to the new edition. “But it is also embryonic and full of Rohmerian moments. It takes on all the themes that will become more developed, complex and impactful in his films.”
points: English translation of Élisabeth, the New Wave director’s 1946 book about young lovers in prewar Paris, receives rave reviews as precursor to auteur’s cinematic work.

articles.title: Nigel Havers: ‘My biggest disappointment? Not playing James Bond’
articles.summary: The actor on mucking out pigs as a teenager, an apology to his first wife and what makes him cry all the time. Born in London, Nigel Havers, 74, was Bafta-nominated for his 1981 role in Chariots of Fire. His other films include A Passage to India and Empire of the Sun.
body: What is your greatest fear? Every actor has the same fear – ie, you’re never going to work again.
What is your earliest memory? Being in a pram in London and there being a road accident ahead and saying to my mother, “Go quickly, I want to see what’s happened.”
Which living person do you most admire, and why? The king – because he’s been through quite a bit and I think he’s come out the other side brilliantly.
What is the trait you most deplore in others? When they don’t tell the truth.

articles.summary: Starring in HBO Max’s “Dune: Prophecy” has been a major “departure” for Emily Watson, whose lauded career was built upon major independent and arthouse successes such as Lars von Trier’s “Breaking the Waves” and Robert Altman’s “Gosford Park.” As she embarks on a second season of the hit show, the…
body: “It was a true departure for me to be in a spaceship,” she said. “You know, it’s actually really good fun.” Speaking about reprising her role as Valya Harkonnen in the upcoming second season of the series, which has been shot but still has no release date, Watson said she experienced a “sense of being on a quest in a way that actors always get to do and actresses don’t. And that was just fun.”

Asked if she could share anything about the highly secretive series, the actress offered a brief tease: “There are a lot of new elements, really interesting and intriguing things I think my head will blow off if I mention any of them,” she quipped.

What about another major upcoming entry in the “Dune” world with Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part Three”? “I mean, I can’t wait to see that movie,” she promptly responded. “I’m a huge fan of him, obviously, and it’s stuffed full of incredible actors that I love.”

articles.title: Stand By Me at 40: Rob Reiner’s seminal coming-of-age saga remains a bittersweet triumph
articles.summary: The late director’s sensitive and detailed adaptation of Stephen King’s novella has an authenticity that so many imitators could never replicate. Coming-of-age metaphors don’t get any blunter than a group of preteen boys following a set of railroad tracks to a classmate’s dead body, a sobering…
body: Though set a few years earlier than American Graffiti, Stand By Me feels like a natural companion to it, another radio-friendly nostalgia piece about a transitional moment for male friends in small-town America. Both films are death-haunted but the difference is that the characters in American Graffiti, who are reaching young adulthood at the cusp of the Vietnam war, don’t know what the future holds and writer-director George Lucas saves that bummer news for the epilogue. The boys in Reiner’s film know what lies at the end of a 20- to 30-mile hike down the tracks and their attraction to the novelty and notoriety of seeing a dead peer turns morbid. Their steps grow heavier by the hour.
points: The late director’s sensitive and detailed adaptation of Stephen King’s novella has an authenticity that so many imitators could never replicate.

articles.title: ‘Everything That’s Wrong With You’ Review: A Luminous Two-Hander from Slovenia About Online Pals Navigating the Waters of IRL Friendship
articles.summary: Anyone with a scrolling habit will know that social media can be a soothing place for the downbeat and lonely. Yet the intimacy you can strike up with strangers rubs up against the uncomfortable fact that our online personae are always manipulated to an extent.
body: Bowing in competition at Sarajevo, the tender sophomore feature by writer-director Urša Menart is anchored by the sweet-and-sour chemistry of stars Klara Kuk and Anuša Kodelja.

Against the backdrop of this handsomely melancholic coastal setting, whose empty offseason cinematographer Roy Van Egmond captures in desaturated pearl-blue tones, “Everything That’s Wrong You” tracks the transition of the women’s friendship from the screen realm to the more precarious IRL one. At first disaster seems likely when wild-child Maruša shows up to Alja’s neatly maintained apartment unannounced, startlingly blasé about imposing her company through the New Year festivities.

The camera loves Maruša’s pink-puffer-clad dachshund a bit too much, so the duo’s climactic fallout unfolds just as expected, and with a resolution that borders on situational comedy. Menart’s script does a fine job of building out these jagged women with a sharp eye for the growing pains of flesh-and-bones relationships born from the seed of virtual connection. It’s the winsome performers that give this modest film an extra punch to perhaps launch it beyond its regional context.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo Releases ‘Handmaid’s Tale’-Inspired Song, ‘Serena Joy,’ in a Tiny Run of CDs, With Digital Drop to Follow
articles.summary: It was already clear Olivia Rodrigo is in full feminist mode these days, with her all-female music festival, Daisy Chain Fields, set to take place in California’s Orange County next Saturday.
body: The existence of a song titled “Serena Joy” had already been confirmed by Rodrigo in June, after fans spotted the title in a studio photograph listing 18 songs that were under consideration for her “You Look Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love” album.

Asked about it in a video interview with Etalk two months ago, Rodrigo smiled and said, “I actually really love [“Serena Joy”]. It didn’t fit on the album. The record was very much a chronicle of a relationship — beginning, middle and end. But I hope that it’ll be a part of something else down the line.”

On Friday morning, Analog Music Shop posted about the song and its exclusive availability. “When we heard that Olivia Rodrigo was bringing an all-women music festival to Orange County, we were honestly just excited to see something this special happening right here in our hometown” (using “hometown” loosely, but close enough, since Tustin is adjacent to Irvine, where Daisy Chain Fields is taking place). “As one of the closest record stores in the area, we wanted to find a way to support Daisy Chain Fields.”

articles.title: Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Wins Best Film in Sarajevo, Ana Urushadze Crowned Best Director
articles.summary: The jury at this year's Sarajevo Film Festival included British actress Emily Watson, European Film Academy director Matthijs Wouter Knol and Yorgos Lanthimos’ producer Athina Rachel Tsangari.
body: Sandra Wollner’s Everytime has been awarded the Honorary Heart for best narrative feature film at the 32nd Sarajevo Film Festival.

As this year’s edition drew to a close on Friday night, filmmakers gathered at the city’s National Theatre where the jury members — including Igor Bezinović, Sara Klimoska, Matthijs Wouter Knol and Athina Rachel Tsangari, led by Emily Watson — unveiled their top picks.

A final Honorary Heart of Sarajevo was awarded to Emir Hadžihafizbegović, one of the most prominent actors in Bosnian-Herzegovinian and regional cinema, in recognition of his contribution to film. He joined Watson, Diego Luna, Woody Harrelson and Asghar Farhadi in receiving an Honorary Heart. The festival officially closed with a screening of a restored No Man’s Land by Danis Tanović. articles.title: David Harbour has blown Tony Stark’s cover in Avengers: Doomsday. It might just be what Marvel needs
articles.summary: The actor, who plays Red Guardian in the film, made a cryptic comment to Variety that raised more Robert Downey Jr-shaped questions than answers. But was it a clanger, or expert trolling? Nobody knows exactly what solemn blood oaths Marvel uses to prevent spoilers.
body: Invited by Variety magazine to offer up a line from Doomsday “completely out of context”, Harbour thought for a moment, adopted the Russian accent of his Red Guardian character and came out with: “You … are Tony Stark.” Which is quite a thing to say about a film whose entire marketing campaign so far has depended on us accepting that Iron Man remains dead, and that the actor who used to play him, Robert Downey Jr, is playing Victor von Doom instead.

So what’s going on? The simplest and most likely explanation is that Harbour is trolling us, that Stark is not in the movie at all, and we’re all just fools. The new trailer for Doomsday, premiered last weekend at Disney’s D23 event in Anaheim, leans heavily into the prevailing wisdom that the film’s villain will be the tyrannical, unstoppable baddie of spurious eastern European extraction that Stan Lee and Jack Kirby dreamed up in 1962.

body: Julio is a Senior Author for Collider. He studied History and International Relations at university, but found his calling in cultural journalism. When he isn't writing, Julio also teaches English at a nearby school. He has lived in São Paulo most of his life, where he covers CCXP and other big events. Having loved movies, music, and TV from an early age, he prides himself in knowing every minute detail about the things he loves. When he is older, he dreams of owning a movie theater in a small countryside town.

When Heroes first premiered in 2006, " Save the cheerleader, save the world " was repeated ad nauseam among viewers and in marketing pieces, making it one of the most celebrated phrases in 2000s pop culture. It was one of the many things about the series that stuck with the audience, one of the first things people usually remember about it, and the simplest way to describe the story, really, as the cheerleader in question, Claire Bennet (played by the late and great Hayden Panettiere ), plays a pivotal role.
